**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 26, verses 10–22:**

(p-118) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And [remember] when your Lord called out to Moses﴾. The meaning is: recite this story to your people.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that they deny me﴾. The ya' of "yukadhdhibuni" (they deny me) is elided, and similarly in ﴿that they kill me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 14], ﴿He will guide me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 62], ﴿Then He guides me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 78], ﴿and gives me drink﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 79], ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 80], ﴿then He will give me life﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 81], ﴿they denied me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 117], and ﴿and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 108]. These are eight verses in which Ya'qub (al-Hadrami, a reader of the Qur'an) affirmed the ya' in both states (in pause and in continuation).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and my chest tightens﴾, that is, because of their denying me, ﴿and my tongue is not loosed﴾, because of the impediment that was in his tongue. Ya'qub read ﴿and it tightens﴾ and ﴿is not loosed﴾ with a fatha on the qaf in both. ﴿So send [word] to Harun﴾: the meaning is that he should help me. The object was elided because the context indicates it. ﴿And they have against me a charge of a crime﴾, which is the man he struck and killed. The meaning is: they have against me a claim of a crime. ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ for it. ﴿He said, "No!"﴾ This is a rebuke and a restraint from remaining in this assumption. The meaning is: they will not kill you, because I will not give them power over you. ﴿So go, you and your brother﴾, meaning: you and your brother. ﴿With Our signs﴾, which are the miracles given to the two of them. ﴿Indeed, We﴾, meaning Himself, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿are with you﴾; He used the plural form for Himself. ﴿[We are] listening﴾: We hear what you both say and what they answer you with.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: "rasul" (messenger) may be used with the meaning of a plural, as in His saying ﴿These are my guests﴾ [Al-Hijr: 68] and His saying ﴿Then We bring you out as a child﴾ [Al-Hajj: 5]. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "We are the message (risala) of the Lord of the worlds," that is, "possessors of the message of the Lord of the worlds." The poet said:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not confide to them any secret, nor did I send them with a message."

That is, with a message (risala).

(p-119) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that you send﴾: the meaning is: that you send ﴿with us the Children of Israel﴾, that is, release them from enslavement. They came to him and conveyed the message. ﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾, that is, a small infant ﴿and you remained among us for years of your life﴾. There are three opinions about this.

The first: eighteen years, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: forty years, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: thirty years, said by Muqatil. The meaning is: you repaid us for raising you by denying our blessing and killing a soul from among us. This is His saying ﴿and you did your deed﴾, which is the killing of a soul. Al-Farra' said: the fa' is given a fatha because it is a single occurrence; if it were intended as something like "a sitting" or "a walking" (i.e., a repeated type of action), its kasra would be permissible.

Regarding His saying ﴿and you are of the disbelievers﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: "of the disbelievers" in My blessing, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. The second: "of the disbelievers" in your god, you were with us in our religion that you now criticize, said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi. According to the first, the meaning is: "and you are now of the disbelievers." According to the second, the meaning is: "and you were."

Regarding His saying ﴿and I am of the astray﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: "of the ignorant," said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada. Some exegetes said: the meaning is that I was ignorant, and nothing from Allah had yet come to me. The second: "of the mistaken," meaning: I killed the soul by mistake, said by Ibn Zayd. The third: "of the forgetful," and a similar usage is His saying ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [Al-Baqara: 282], said by Abu 'Ubayda.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So I fled from you﴾, that is, I departed from among you ﴿when I feared you﴾ for (p-120) my own self, to Madyan. 'Asim al-Jahdari, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ya'mur read "lamma" (when) with a kasra on the lam and a lightened mim. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgment﴾, and there are two opinions regarding it.

The first: prophethood, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: knowledge and understanding, said by Muqatil.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And is this a blessing with which you remind me﴾, meaning the upbringing ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, that is, you have made them slaves. It is said: "'abbadtu fulanan," "a'badtuhu," and "asta'badtuhu," meaning: I took him as a slave.

Regarding "an" (that), there are two possibilities.

The first: it may be in a nominative position as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution or apposition) for "ni'ma" (blessing). The second: it may be in an accusative position by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid, the dropping of a governing preposition), its estimate being "because you enslaved," or "for your enslaving."

The scholars differed in interpreting the verse. Some interpreted it as a denial (inkar), and others as an affirmation (iqrar).

Whoever interpreted it as a denial said the meaning of the statement is: "Is that a blessing?!" in the form of a question, like His saying ﴿This is my lord﴾ [Al-An'am: 76], and His saying ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 34]. They recited:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her eyelid was full of her tears,"

"And her saying, while the riding-camels were moving, 'You leave us like this and go away?'"

(p-121) This is the view of a group of them. Then they have four opinions regarding the meaning and its interpretation.

The first: that Pharaoh took the wealth of the Children of Israel, enslaved them, and spent on Moses from it. So Moses cancelled the blessing, because it was the wealth of the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the meaning is: if you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my family would have raised me, and my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So it is as though you are reminding me of a favor for which your trial was the cause. This is the view of al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and al-Azhari.

The third: the meaning is: do you remind me of your kindness to me alone, while forgetting your wrongdoing in enslaving the Children of Israel?! This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: the meaning is: how do you remind me of the upbringing when you have enslaved my people?! Whoever has his people humiliated has been humiliated, so your kindness to me has been nullified by your enslaving my people. This was related by al-Tha'labi.

As for whoever interpreted it as an affirmation, he said: Moses counted it a blessing that he raised him and did not kill him nor enslave him. The meaning is: indeed, by my life, it is a blessing that you raised me and did not enslave me as you enslaved the Children of Israel. So "an" indicates an elided element. A comparable usage in speech is: that you strike some of your slaves and leave the other, so the one left says: "This is a blessing for me, that you struck so-and-so and left me," and then "and left me" is elided because the meaning is known. This is the view of al-Farra'.

According to the first, the meaning is: "and you are now of the disbelievers." According to the second, the meaning is: "and you were."

Regarding His saying ﴿and I am of the astray﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: "of the ignorant," said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada. Some exegetes said: the meaning is that I was ignorant, and nothing from Allah had yet come to me. The second: "of the mistaken," meaning: I killed the soul by mistake, said by Ibn Zayd. The third: "of the forgetful," and a similar usage is His saying ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [Al-Baqara: 282], said by Abu 'Ubayda.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So I fled from you﴾, that is, I departed from among you ﴿when I feared you﴾ for (p-120) my own self, to Madyan. 'Asim al-Jahdari, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ya'mur read "lamma" (when) with a kasra on the lam and a lightened mim. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgment﴾, and there are two opinions regarding it.

The first: prophethood, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: knowledge and understanding, said by Muqatil.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And is this a blessing with which you remind me﴾, meaning the upbringing ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, that is, you have made them slaves. It is said: "'abbadtu fulanan," "a'badtuhu," and "asta'badtuhu," meaning: I took him as a slave.

Regarding "an" (that), there are two possibilities.

The first: it may be in a nominative position as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution or apposition) for "ni'ma" (blessing). The second: it may be in an accusative position by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid, the dropping of a governing preposition), its estimate being "because you enslaved," or "for your enslaving."

The scholars differed in interpreting the verse. Some interpreted it as a denial (inkar), and others as an affirmation (iqrar).

Whoever interpreted it as a denial said the meaning of the statement is: "Is that a blessing?!" in the form of a question, like His saying ﴿This is my lord﴾ [Al-An'am: 76], and His saying ﴿So are they the ones who will abide forever?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 34]. They recited:

"I have not forgotten the day of departure, her standing, and her eyelid was full of her tears,"

"And her saying, while the riding-camels were moving, 'You leave us like this and go away?'"

(p-121) This is the view of a group of them. Then they have four opinions regarding the meaning and its interpretation.

The first: that Pharaoh took the wealth of the Children of Israel, enslaved them, and spent on Moses from it. So Moses cancelled the blessing, because it was the wealth of the Children of Israel. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the meaning is: if you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my family would have raised me, and my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So it is as though you are reminding me of a favor for which your trial was the cause. This is the view of al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and al-Azhari.

The third: the meaning is: do you remind me of your kindness to me alone, while forgetting your wrongdoing in enslaving the Children of Israel?! This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: the meaning is: how do you remind me of the upbringing when you have enslaved my people?! Whoever has his people humiliated has been humiliated, so your kindness to me has been nullified by your enslaving my people. This was related by al-Tha'labi.

As for whoever interpreted it as an affirmation, he said: Moses counted it a blessing that he raised him and did not kill him nor enslave him. The meaning is: indeed, by my life, it is a blessing that you raised me and did not enslave me as you enslaved the Children of Israel. So "an" indicates an elided element. A comparable usage in speech is: that you strike some of your slaves and leave the other, so the one left says: "This is a blessing for me, that you struck so-and-so and left me," and then "and left me" is elided because the meaning is known. This is the view of al-Farra'.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 26, verses 10–22:**

(p-118) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And [remember] when your Lord called out to Moses﴾. The meaning is: recite this story to your people.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that they deny me﴾. The ya' of "yukadhdhibuni" (they deny me) is elided, and similarly in ﴿that they kill me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 14], ﴿He will guide me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 62], ﴿Then He guides me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 78], ﴿and gives me drink﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 79], ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 80], ﴿then He will give me life﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 81], ﴿they denied me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 117], and ﴿and obey me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 108]. These are eight verses in which Ya'qub (al-Hadrami, a reader of the Qur'an) affirmed the ya' in both states (in pause and in continuation).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and my chest tightens﴾, that is, because of their denying me, ﴿and my tongue is not loosed﴾, because of the impediment that was in his tongue. Ya'qub read ﴿and it tightens﴾ and ﴿is not loosed﴾ with a fatha on the qaf in both. ﴿So send [word] to Harun﴾: the meaning is that he should help me. The object was elided because the context indicates it. ﴿And they have against me a charge of a crime﴾, which is the man he struck and killed. The meaning is: they have against me a claim of a crime. ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ for it. ﴿He said, "No!"﴾ This is a rebuke and a restraint from remaining in this assumption. The meaning is: they will not kill you, because I will not give them power over you. ﴿So go, you and your brother﴾, meaning: you and your brother. ﴿With Our signs﴾, which are the miracles given to the two of them. ﴿Indeed, We﴾, meaning Himself, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿are with you﴾; He used the plural form for Himself. ﴿[We are] listening﴾: We hear what you both say and what they answer you with.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾. That is, with a message (risala).

(p-124) Qur'an 26:29 onward, Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Even if I came to you with something clear?﴾ That is, with a matter manifest, by which you would recognize my truthfulness. "Will you imprison me?!" The rest of this is explained in Al-A'raf (Al-A'raf: 107), up to His saying: ﴿So the magicians were gathered for an appointed day known﴾, and it was the Day of Adornment, which was a festival for them. ﴿And it was said to the people﴾, meaning the people of Egypt. Ibn Zayd held that their gathering took place at Alexandria.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That we may follow the magicians﴾. Most scholars said: they meant the magicians of Pharaoh, so the meaning is, "That we may follow them in their affair." Others said: they meant Musa and Harun, and they only said this in mockery. Ibn Jarir said: "la'alla" (perhaps, so that) here has the meaning of "kay" (in order that). His saying: ﴿in the might of Pharaoh﴾ means: in his greatness.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 49–51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then you will come to know﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam (al-lam, the emphatic lam) has entered for emphasis (tawkid, emphasis).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿No harm﴾, meaning: no injury. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is from darra-hu yadurru-hu and yadir-hu, meaning: he harmed him. The meaning is: there is no harm upon us in what befalls us in this world, because we are returning to our Lord in the Hereafter, hoping for His forgiveness.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That we were﴾, meaning: because we were ﴿the first of the believers﴾ in the signs of Musa in this situation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 52–59:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you will be followed﴾, meaning: Pharaoh and his people will pursue you.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, these﴾. The meaning: Pharaoh said, "Indeed, these," meaning the Children of Israel, ﴿are a small band﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a group (ṭā'ifah). Al-Zajjaj said: al-shirdhimah (a small number) in the speech of the Arabs means "the few." The commentators said: they were six hundred thousand, but he belittled them by comparison to his army, which could not be counted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. You say: "al-shay' ghaṭaṇī" (the thing enraged me) when it angers you.

Ibn Jarir said: It is mentioned that their rage was because of the killing by the angels of their firstborn sons.

He said: It is also possible that their rage was due to the loss of the borrowed ornaments they had taken from their jewelry, and it is possible that it was due to their separation from them and their departure from their land against their will.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, we are all alert and wary﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited "ḥadhirūn" without an alif. The rest recited "ḥādhirūn" with an alif. Is there a difference between them? There are two views.

One: that the ḥādhir (alert, wary) is the one who is prepared, and the ḥadhir is the one who is watchful. It has come in the tafsir that the meaning of ḥādhirīn is "mu'did" (armed), i.e., possessors of equipment (adah), which is weapons, because they are the instruments of war.

The second: that they are two dialects with the same meaning. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is said, "rajul ḥadhir, ḥadhur, and ḥādhir" (a man who is wary). And al-maqam al-karim: the good dwelling.

Regarding His saying, ﴿Thus﴾, there are two views.

One: "Thus I will do to those who disobey me," related by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: "The matter is thus," that is, as We have described, related by al-Zajjaj.

(p-126) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾. That is because Allah, Exalted is He, returned them to Egypt after Pharaoh's drowning, and gave them what had belonged to Pharaoh and his people of dwellings and wealth.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: He made the abodes of the family of Pharaoh a possession for the Children of Israel, but He did not return them to them; rather He made their dwellings in al-Sham.

**Verse 60:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So they pursued them﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: they caught up with them, ﴿at sunrise﴾, meaning when the sun had risen, that is, had come up. It is said: "Ashraqna" means we entered the time of sunrise (ash-shuruq), just as it is said "amsayna" and "asbahna" (we entered the evening and the morning).

Al-Hasan and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read ﴿fa-ittaba'uhum﴾ with the doubled letter (shaddah), "fattaba'uhum."

**Verse 61:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When the two hosts saw each other﴾. Abu Raja', al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read "tarra'a" (تَرِاأى) with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the hamza, meaning they came face to face, so that each party saw the other.

**Verse 62:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Never! Surely my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. That is: they will never overtake us. ﴿He will guide me﴾ means He will show me the way to salvation.

**Verse 63:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then he struck, and it parted﴾. There is an implied element here: "so he struck, and it parted." That is, the water split into twelve paths. ﴿And each part was like a mighty mountain﴾: each portion that had split off from it. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and Asim al-Jahdari read "kullu filq" (كُلُّ فِلْقٍ) with a lam, (a recitation variant) meaning each cleft. ﴿Like a mighty mountain﴾ means like a mountain (al-jabal).

**Verse 64:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾. That is: We brought the others near to the drowning, and they were the companions of Pharaoh. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "azlafna" means "we gathered." Al-Zajjaj said: Both opinions are sound, because gathering them is bringing some of them near to others, and the basic meaning of "al-zulfa" in the Arabic language is nearness (al-qurba).

Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', al-Dahhak and Ibn Ya'mur read "azlaqna" (أزلقنا) with a qaf. They also read ﴿And the Garden was brought near﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 90] with a qaf in the same way.

**Verse 67:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Surely in that is a sign﴾, meaning: in the destruction of Pharaoh and his people there is a lesson for those who come after them. ﴿And most of them were not believers﴾: that is, most of the people of Egypt were not believers. Only Asiya believed, and Khirbil, the believer from the family of Pharaoh, and Finna the hairdresser, and Maryam, the woman who guided Musa to the bones of Yusuf. This is the statement of Muqatil.

Whatever words in the story of Musa I have left unexplained have already been explained earlier. Likewise, whatever mention is missing in one place is either something that has already been covered or is evident. So be attentive to this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 69–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they hear you﴾ The meaning: do they hear your supplication? Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Ya'mur, and Asim al-Jahdari read: "Do they make you hear" (hal yusmi'unakum), with a dammah on the ya' and a kasrah on the mim. ﴿When you call﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: if you wish, you may make the dhal clear, or you may assimilate it into the ta', and the latter is better in Arabic, because the dhal is close to the ta' (in articulation).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?﴾ That is: if you worship them, or if you do not worship them, do they harm you? So they reported about the imitation of their fathers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ There are two views concerning this.

The first: its wording is singular, but what is meant is plural; so the meaning is: indeed they are enemies to me.

The second: indeed every object of worship of yours is an enemy to me.

If it is asked: what is the reason for describing inanimate objects with enmity?

The answer is in two respects. The first: its meaning is: indeed they will be an enemy to me on the Day of Resurrection, if I worship them. The second: that it is of the inverted form (maqlub); and the meaning is: indeed I am an enemy to them, because whoever you oppose, opposes you. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Concerning His saying ﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾ there are two views.

The first: that it is an exception from the genus, because he knew that they used to worship Allah along with their deities; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is an exception from a different genus; and the meaning is: but the Lord of the worlds [is not like that]; this was said by most of the grammarians.

(p-129) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾ That is: to right guidance, not what you worship. ﴿And He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ That is: He is the one who provides me with food and drink.

If it is asked: why did he say ﴿I am ill﴾ and did not say "He made me ill"?

The answer is: he intended to praise his Lord, so he attributed to Him pure good; for if he had said "He made me ill," his people would have considered that a defect. Thus he employed good manners. A parallel to this is the story of al-Khidr, when he said concerning the defect: ﴿So I intended﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], and concerning the pure good: ﴿So your Lord intended﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

If it is asked: but this is refuted by His saying ﴿And He who causes me to die﴾.

The answer is: the people did not deny death, but they attributed to it a cause other than the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So Ibrahim attributed it to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. His saying ﴿then He gives me life﴾ means for the resurrection, [and this is] a matter they did not acknowledge; he said it only as an argument against them. The meaning: that in which you agreed with me necessitates the soundness of my statement in what you disagreed with me about.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He who I hope will forgive me my sin﴾ means: what befalls the likes of me of slips; and the exegetes say: he only meant the three statements we mentioned in (al-Anbiya: 63). ﴿On the Day of Judgment﴾ means: the Day of Gathering and Reckoning. This is an argument against his people that divinity is fitting only for one who does these deeds.

(p-129) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾ That is: to right guidance, not what you worship. ﴿And He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ That is: He is the one who provides me with food and drink.

If it is asked: why did he say ﴿I am ill﴾ and did not say "He made me ill"?

The answer is: he intended to praise his Lord, so he attributed to Him pure good; for if he had said "He made me ill," his people would have considered that a defect. Thus he employed good manners. A parallel to this is the story of al-Khidr, when he said concerning the defect: ﴿So I intended﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], and concerning the pure good: ﴿So your Lord intended﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

If it is asked: but this is refuted by His saying ﴿And He who causes me to die﴾.

The answer is: the people did not deny death, but they attributed to it a cause other than the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So Ibrahim attributed it to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. His saying ﴿then He gives me life﴾ means for the resurrection, [and this is] a matter they did not acknowledge; he said it only as an argument against them. The meaning: that in which you agreed with me necessitates the soundness of my statement in what you disagreed with me about.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He who I hope will forgive me my sin﴾ means: what befalls the likes of me of slips; and the exegetes say: he only meant the three statements we mentioned in (al-Anbiya: 63). ﴿On the Day of Judgment﴾ means: the Day of Gathering and Reckoning. This is an argument against his people that divinity is fitting only for one who does these deeds.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Grant me wisdom﴾ has three interpretations.

The first is prophethood (nubuwwah), related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The second is intellect (al-lubb), said by Ikrimah. The third is understanding and knowledge (al-fahm wal-'ilm), said by Muqatil. We have already explained His words ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ in Surah Yusuf (101), and we explained the meaning of ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ in Maryam (50). By "the later ones" is meant those who come after him until the Day of Resurrection.

His words ﴿and forgive my father﴾: al-Hasan said, "It has reached me that his mother was a Muslim, following his religion, and therefore he did not mention her."

If it is said: he did say, ﴿Forgive me and my parents﴾ (Ibrahim: 41).

It is answered: most of the mention went to his father, so it is permissible that he asked forgiveness for his mother, who was a believer. As for his father, there is no doubt about his disbelief. We have explained the reason for his seeking forgiveness for his father in Bara'ah (113), and we mentioned the meaning of disgrace (al-khizy) in Al 'Imran (192).

His words ﴿the Day they are raised﴾: meaning the creation.

His words ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ have six interpretations.

The first: sound from shirk (associating partners with God), said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The second: sound from doubt, said by Mujahid.

The third: sound, meaning healthy, and this is the heart of the believer, because the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. Said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The fourth: in the language (lughah), "sound" (salim) means "stung" (ladig). So the meaning is like one stung out of fear of God, Exalted is He. Said by al-Junayd.

The fifth: sound from the afflictions of wealth and children, said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The sixth: sound from innovation (bid'ah), firmly settled upon the Sunnah (the prophetic way), related by al-Tha'labi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 90–104:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, meaning: it will be brought close to them, until they look upon it. ﴿And Hell will be brought forth for the deviators﴾, meaning: it will be made manifest, ﴿for the deviators﴾, who are the astray. ﴿And it will be said to them﴾ in a rebuking manner: ﴿Where is that which you used to worship ﴿besides Allah﴾? Will they help you?﴾, meaning: will they prevent you from the punishment, or will they defend themselves against it?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they will be thrown into it [Hell] headlong﴾. Al-Suddi said: they are the polytheists. Ibn Qutaybah said: they will be cast upon their faces. The original form of the word is "kubbibu," from your saying "kabbabtu al-ina'" (I overturned the vessel), and the middle letter ba' was changed to kaf, due to the disliking of the gathering of three bas, just as they said "kumkimu" from "al-kummah," whose original form is "kummimu." Al-Zajjaj said: (p-132) its meaning is: some of them are thrown upon others. The real meaning of this in the language is the repetition of falling headlong, as if when it is cast down it keeps falling on its face again and again until it settles in it.

Regarding "al-Ghawun" (the deviators) there are three opinions:
One: the polytheists, related by Ibn Abbas.
The second: the devils, related by Qatadah and Muqatil.
The third: the idols, related by al-Suddi.

﴿And the hosts of Iblis all together﴾: his followers from among the jinn and mankind. ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein﴾, meaning: they and their gods. ﴿By Allah, we were certainly in manifest error﴾. Al-Farra' said: "la-qad kunna" (we were indeed). Al-Zajjaj said: we were only in error.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: we made you equal to Allah in worship. ﴿And none led us astray except the criminals﴾. Regarding them there are two opinions:
One: the devils.
The second: their leaders whom they followed. Ikrimah said: Iblis and the son of Adam who committed murder.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾. This is their saying when the prophets, the angels and the believers intercede. Jabir ibn Abdullah related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Indeed a man will say in Paradise: 'What has become of my friend so-and-so?' while his friend is in Hell. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, will say: 'Bring out his friend to Paradise.' Then those who remain [in the Fire] will say: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a loyal friend﴾?"

Al-Hamim: the close relative whom you love and who loves you. The meaning: we have no (p-133) relative who is concerned with our affair. ﴿So if only we had a return﴾, meaning: a return to the world, ﴿and we would be among the believers﴾, so that intercession would be permitted for us just as it was permitted for the monotheists.

The second: their leaders whom they followed. Ikrimah said: Iblis and the son of Adam who committed murder.

Jabir ibn Abdullah related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Indeed a man will say in Paradise: 'What has become of my friend so-and-so?' while his friend is in Hell. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, will say: 'Bring out his friend to Paradise.' Then those who remain [in the Fire] will say: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a loyal friend﴾?"

Al-Hamim: the close relative whom you love and who loves you. The meaning: we have no (p-133) relative who is concerned with our affair. ﴿So if only we had a return﴾, meaning: a return to the world, ﴿and we would be among the believers﴾, so that intercession would be permitted for us just as it was permitted for the monotheists.

"The first: the craftsmen (al-ḥākka, weavers/cloth-workers). Narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 117–122:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So decide between me and them with a decision﴾, meaning: judge between me and them with a judgment, namely by the punishment, ﴿and save me and those with me﴾ from that punishment. The ark (al-fulk) has already been explained [al-Baqarah: 164]. The "mashḥun" (filled, laden) means full, as one says: "shahantu al-inā'" (I filled the vessel) when I filled it. Noah's ship had been filled with people, birds and all kinds of animals, ﴿then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾, after the salvation of Noah and those with him, ﴿the others﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 123–135:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, [doing] pointless [things]?﴾ ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī, Abū Ḥaywa, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "bi-kulli rayʿin" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ (rayʿ). Al-Farrāʾ said: "They are two dialects." Then there are three opinions regarding it.

The first: it is the elevated place. Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Every lofty place (bi-kulli sharaf)." Al-Zajjāj said: "Linguistically, it is the elevated place of the earth."

The second: it is the road. This was narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Qatāda also said so.

The third: it is the wide pass between two mountains. This was said by Mujāhid. And the word āya (﴿monument﴾) means "a sign."

Regarding what they intended by this building, there are three opinions.

The first: they intended, "You build what you do not dwell in." This was narrated by ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās; the meaning is that their building was pointless, for which they had no need.

The second: pigeon-towers (burūj al-ḥamām). This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid.

The third: they used to build in elevated places in order to overlook passersby so that they would mock them and make sport of them. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you take fortresses (maṣāniʿ)﴾ has three opinions.

The first: lofty palaces, said by Mujāhid. The second: water cisterns beneath the earth, said by Qatāda. The third: pigeon-towers, said by al-Suddī.

Regarding His saying: ﴿that perhaps you may abide forever﴾ there are two views.

The first: "as if you were to abide forever," said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Mālik.

The second: "in order that you may abide," said by al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba. ʿIkrima, al-Nakhaʿī, Qatāda, and Ibn Yaʿmur read "takhlodūna" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, the khāʾ sukūn, and the lām light (mukhaffafa). ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Abū Ḥuṣayn read "takhulldūna" with a fatḥa on the khāʾ and a shadda on the lām.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾ The meaning: when you beat, you beat with whips the beating of tyrants, and when you punish, you kill. He only denounced them for this because it proceeded from injustice, since if they had struck with a sword or a whip in a just cause, they would not have been blamed.

Regarding His saying: ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ there are two views.

The first: what they were punished with in this world. The second: the punishment of Hellfire.

(p-137) His words, may He be exalted: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the ancients﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "khalq" with a fatha on the kha' and a sukun on the lam. Ibn Qutayba said: they meant their fabrication and their lying. It is said: "khalaqtu al-hadith" and "ikhtalaqtuhu," meaning I invented the story. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs call fables "ahadith al-khalq" (tales of fabrication). ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, [Khalaf, and Nafi']: "khuluq al-awwalin," with a damma on the kha' and the lam. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, and ʿĀṣim al-Jahdari read "khuluq" with a damma on the kha' and a sukun on the lam; the meaning is their habit and their way. Qatada said: they said to him, "This is how people have lived, as long as they live, then they die, and there is no resurrection for them and no reckoning."

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And we will not be punished﴾, that is, for what we do in this world.

(p-138) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here?﴾ That is: in what Allah has given you in this world, ﴿secure﴾ from death and punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿its spathes are soft and delicate (hadim)﴾. The ṭal‘ is the fruit. Regarding the word hadim there are seven opinions.

The first: it is the fruit that has ripened and matured; narrated by al-‘Awfi from Ibn ‘Abbas. The second: it is that which crumbles readily when crushed; said by Mujahid. The third: it is that which has no pit (stone); said by al-Hasan. The fourth: it is the moist, softened date (rutab) that has been bruised; said by Sa‘id ibn Jubayr. The fifth: it is softness; said by Qatadah and al-Farra’. The sixth: it is the heavy cluster whose fruits press upon one another; said by al-Dahhak. The seventh: it is the spathe before it splits open from its sheath [the husk] and bursts open, meaning that it is closed up and compact; and from this it is said: "a man with a hadim of the two flanks (ahḍam al-kashḥayn)," when they are tightly drawn together; said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you hew out houses from the mountains, skillfully (fariheen)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi‘ and Abu ‘Amr read "fariheen" (without alif). The rest read "farihin" (with an alif). Ibn Qutaybah said: "fariheen" means insolent and exultant. It is also said that the ha’ in it is substituted for a ḥa’, meaning "fariḥīn" (joyful); and "faraḥ" may mean happiness and may mean insolence, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant (al-fariḥīn)﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], meaning the insolent. As for the one who reads "fārihīn," it is another dialect: it is said farih and fārih, just as it is said fariḥ and fāriḥ. It is also said that fārihīn means skilled (ḥādhiqīn); ‘Ikrimah said: skilled in hewing them.

(p-139) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant (al-musrifīn)﴾. Ibn ‘Abbas said: it means the polytheists. Muqatil said: they are the nine men who hamstrung the she-camel.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 165–175:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds?﴾ — "al-dhukrān" is the plural of "dhakar" — meaning, from among the children of Adam. ﴿And leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses?﴾ [al-Zajjaj said: Ibn Mas'ud recited: "what your Lord has made right for you of your spouses."] He means by this the private parts (furuj). Mujahid said: "You have left the fronts of women for the backs of men."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay, you are a transgressing people﴾ — meaning, wrongdoers and aggressors. ﴿They said: "If you do not desist, O Lut﴾ — meaning, if you do not refrain from forbidding us — ﴿you will surely be among those expelled﴾ from our land. ﴿He said: "Indeed, I am, of your deed,﴾ meaning: the coming to males ﴿among those who detest.﴾" Ibn Qutaybah said: meaning, among those who hate, it is said: "qalaytu al-rajul" when I hated the man.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿My Lord, deliver me and my family from what they do﴾ — meaning, from the punishment for their deed. ﴿So We delivered him and his family﴾ — and We have mentioned them in (Hud: 80) — ﴿except an old woman﴾ meaning: his wife ﴿among those who remained behind.﴾ meaning: those who remained in the punishment. ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ We destroyed them by sinking and by stoning, and this is His saying: ﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾ meaning: stones.

(p-141) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The companions of the thicket (Ayka) denied the messengers.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "Ashab Layka" here, and in (Sad: 13) without a hamza, with the taa' vowelled with a fatha; the rest read "al-Ayka" with a hamza in both places and with an alif. This word has already been discussed (al-Hijr: 78).

﴿When Shu'ayb said to them﴾ If it is asked: why did he not say "their brother" (akhuhum), as he said in (al-A'raf: 85)? The answer: Shu'ayb was not of the lineage of the companions of the thicket, so he did not say "their brother." He was sent to them after he had been sent to Madyan, and he was of the lineage of Madyan, so there he said "their brother." This is the view of Muqatil ibn Sulayman. We have mentioned in Surah Hud (94), from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, that the people of Madyan were punished with the punishment of the shade-cloud. If they were other than the companions of the thicket, as Muqatil claims, then they were equal in the punishment; and if the companions of Madyan were the companions of the thicket, which is the position of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, then the omission of mentioning the brother was for brevity. And God knows best.

(p-142) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among those who cause loss﴾, that is, among those who diminish in measuring. It is said: "akhsartu al-kayl wa al-wazn" (I caused loss in the measure and the weight) when one diminishes it. We have already mentioned the qistas (balance) in (Surat Bani Isra'il: 35).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear the One who created you and the jibilla﴾, that is, and the One who created the jibilla.

It was also said: the meaning is: "remember what befell the jibilla of the former ones" ﴿the former ones﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa al-jibillatu" with a damma on the jim and the ba' both, with the lam doubled. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Dahhak, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read it with a kasra on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a light lam. Ibn Qutayba said: al-jibilla means the creation; it is said: "jubila fulan 'ala kadha" (so-and-so was created upon such-and-such), meaning he was created. The poet said:

"And death is the greatest of calamities that passes over the jibilla."

Ibn Qutayba said: al-jibilla means the creation; it is said: "jubila fulan 'ala kadha" (so-and-so was created upon such-and-such), meaning he was created. The poet said:

"And death is the greatest of calamities that passes over the jibilla."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verses 185–191:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So make a piece of the sky fall upon us﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a piece ﴿from the sky﴾, and "kisaf" is the plural of "kisfah," just as it is said "qita'" and "qit'ah."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My Lord is most knowing of what you do﴾. That is, of the shortfall in measure and weight. The meaning is: He will recompense you if He wills, and your punishment is not in my hand. ﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them﴾. The exegetes said: God sent upon them an intense heat, which seized their breaths, so they came out of their houses fleeing into the desert. God then sent upon them a cloud that shaded them from the sun, and they found coolness in it, and they called out to one another. When they gathered beneath it, God sent upon them fire, and that was among the greatest of punishments. "Al-Zullah" is the cloud that shaded them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verse 192–199:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ That is, the Qur'an. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit (al-Ruh al-Amin) has brought it down.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Hafs from 'Asim read: "nazala bihi" (lightly, with the verb unstressed) and "al-Ruhu al-Aminu" (with a raised, nominative ending). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "nazzala" (with the zay doubled) and "al-Ruha al-Amina" (with an accusative ending). By "the Trustworthy Spirit" is meant Jibril, who is trustworthy concerning the revelation of Allah Exalted to His prophets. ﴿Upon your heart.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it descended upon you, and your heart retained it, so it became firm, and you will never forget it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that you may be among the warners.﴾ That is, among those who warn with the signs of Allah the deniers. ﴿In a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: in the tongue of Quraysh, so that they may understand what is in it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.﴾ Al-A'mash read: "zubri" with the ba' sukun. Regarding the pronoun of reference (ha' al-kinayah) there are two views.

The first: it refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is: indeed the mention of the Qur'an and its report is in the earlier scriptures. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as stated by Muqatil. And "al-zubur" means the books.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: "awa lam yakun lahum" with the ya' and "ayatan" with the accusative. Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "takun" with the ta' and "ayatun" with the nominative. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Qatadah read: "takun" with the ta' and "ayatan" with the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: if you say "yakun" with the ya', the preferred reading is to put "ayatan" in the accusative, with "an" as the subject of "kana" and "ayatun" as its predicate. The meaning: Has it not been a sign for them, the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel, that the Prophet ﷺ is true and that his prophethood is true? "Ayah" means a clear sign, because the scholars among the Children of Israel who believed found the mention of the Prophet ﷺ written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. As for the one who reads "awa lam takun" with the ta', he makes "ayatun" the subject and "an ya'lamahu" the predicate of "takun".

It is also permissible to read "awa lam takun" with the ta' and "ayatan" with the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿Then their trial would not have been [anything] but...﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read: "an ta'lamahu" with the ta'.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of Makkah sent to the Jews, who were in Madinah, asking them about Muhammad ﷺ. They said: "Indeed, this is his time, and we find his description in the Torah." That was a sign for them of his truthfulness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Upon some of the non-Arabs.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of a'jam, the feminine being 'ajma', and al-a'jam is one who does not speak clearly; likewise al-a'jami. As for al-'ajami, it is one who is of the stock of the non-Arabs, whether he speaks clearly or not.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they would not have been believers in it.﴾ That is: if a non-Arab had recited it to them, they would have said, "We do not understand this," and so they would not have believed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verses 200–209:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus did We make it enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾. We have explained this in (Surat al-Hijr: 12). The criminals here are the polytheists.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not believe in it﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so that they do not believe." As for the painful punishment, it is at the time of death. ﴿So they will say﴾ at the descent of the punishment ﴿Are we to be reprieved?﴾ meaning: are we to be delayed so that we may believe and affirm? Muqatil said: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threatened them with the punishment, they said: "Then when is it?" denying it, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then, is it Our punishment they are hastening?﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered, if We let them enjoy for years﴾. ʿIkrimah said: the lifespan of the world.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then there comes to them what they were promised﴾, meaning: of the punishment. ﴿And We did not destroy any town﴾ with punishment in this world ﴿except that it had warners﴾, meaning: messengers warning them of the punishment. ﴿A reminder﴾, meaning: an admonition and a reminding.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the devils have not brought it down﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab nuzuliha) was that the Quraysh said: "The devils only bring the Qur'an and cast it upon the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So this verse was revealed. Related by Muqatil.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And it is not suitable for them﴾, meaning: that they should bring down the Qur'an. ﴿Nor are they able﴾ to bring it from the heaven, because they have been barred from hearing it by the angels and the shooting stars. ﴿Indeed, they are removed from the hearing﴾, meaning: removed from listening to the revelation from the heaven. ﴿So how could they bring it down?!﴾ And ʿAṭāʾ said: "They are indeed debarred from hearing the Qur'an, because they are pelted with the stars."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 26, verses 224–227:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the poets, those who go astray follow them﴾. Nafi' recited "yutbiuhum" (يُتْبِعُهم) with a sukun on the taa'. Both readings are good. It is said: tabi'tu and ittaba'tu (تَبِعْتُ واتَّبَعْتُ), like haqqartu and ihtaqartu (حَقَّرْتُ واحْتَقَرْتُ).

Al-Awfi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: There were two men in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who had exchanged satire, and each of them had with him misguided people from his tribe. So Allah said: ﴿And the poets, those who go astray follow them﴾. In another narration from Ibn Abbas, he said: They are the poets of the polytheists. Muqatil said: Among them were Abdullah ibn al-Zaba'ra, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb al-Makhzumi, along with others. They said: "We say the same as what Muhammad says," and they composed poetry. Misguided people from their tribes gathered around them, listening to their poetry and transmitting it from them.

Regarding "those who go astray" (al-ghawun, الغاوِينَ) there are three opinions. The first: they are the devils, as said by Mujahid and Qatadah. The second: they are the foolish, as said by al-Dahhak. The third: they are the polytheists, as said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a parable for one who wanders in the valleys. The meaning is that they take up every kind of idle talk, lies and other things. They praise with falsehood and blame with falsehood, and they say "we did" when they did not do.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Except those who believe﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "When the censure of the poets was revealed, Ka'b ibn Malik, Abdullah ibn Rawahah and Hassan ibn Thabit came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has revealed this while He knows that we are poets.' Then this verse was revealed." The commentators said: This exception is for the Muslim poets who praised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and defended him from satire. ﴿And remember Allah often﴾, i.e., poetry did not distract them from the remembrance of Allah, and they did not make poetry their concern. Ibn Zayd said: "And they remembered Allah in their poetry." It was also said: the intended remembrance is poetry in obedience to Allah, mighty and majestic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they defended themselves﴾, i.e., against the polytheists, ﴿after they had been wronged﴾, because the polytheists began with satire. Then He threatened the poets of the polytheists, saying: ﴿And those who did wrong will know what [kind of] return they will be returned to﴾, i.e., those who associated partners with Allah and satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. ﴿Ayya munqalabin yanqalibun﴾ (أيَّ مُنْقَلَبٍ يَنْقَلِبُونَ).
